authors: Amira Abdu, M Erin Henry, Nicole M André, Andrew D Miller, Manigandan Lejeune, Elizabeth A Berliner, Gary R Whittaker
journal: Veterinary Parasitology: Regional Studies and Reports

mcqs.q: A failure-to-thrive shelter kitten with progressive neurologic signs was clinically suspected to have non-effusive FIP. What ultimately established the true diagnosis?
o: Necropsy histopathology with Toxoplasma PCR confirmation
mcqs.e: Diagnosis required postmortem brain histopathology showing Toxoplasma bradyzoites/tachyzoites, confirmed by PCR.

mcqs.q: What did molecular testing for feline coronavirus reveal in this case?
o: Necropsy molecular testing found no feline coronavirus
Serology was strongly positive for coronavirus
mcqs.e: No feline coronavirus was detected; overwhelming toxoplasmosis, not FIP, was the cause.

mcqs.q: For neurologic signs in a failure-to-thrive shelter kitten, which should remain on the differential alongside FIP?
mcqs.e: The authors stress keeping toxoplasmosis and portosystemic shunt in mind, noting antemortem diagnosis is limited in resource-poor shelters.

authors: Emily D Dolan, Brett Wyker, Elizabeth A Berliner, Matt Goldweber, Ana Hernandez

mcqs.q: What is the central argument of this One Health commentary?
o: Pets should be excluded from public health data to reduce confounding
Pets should be explicitly included in public health research and policy
Public health should focus only on humans
mcqs.e: The piece argues companion animals must be incorporated into public health research, data, and policy because they are integral to family and community wellbeing.

mcqs.q: According to the authors, excluding pets from public health support services creates:
o: Gaps in support services for families and communities
mcqs.e: Leaving pets out of support systems creates gaps because pets are integral to the wellbeing of families and communities.

mcqs.q: This article is best described as:
o: An editorial / One Health call to action
mcqs.e: It is an editorial/commentary framed as a One Health call to action, with no structured abstract.

mcqs.q: Why do the authors consider criminal cruelty statutes limited for protecting hoarded animals?
o: They are reactive, requiring harm before intervention
They are purely civil in nature
mcqs.e: Cruelty statutes are largely reactive ('some must suffer first'), so intervention lags behind foreseeable harm.

mcqs.q: What approach do the authors propose as better protecting animals in hoarding cases?
o: Doing nothing until substantial harm occurs
A civil forfeiture approach paired with mental health intervention
mcqs.e: They favor a civil/forfeiture route with mental health intervention over reactive criminal prosecution.

mcqs.q: Animal hoarding deficits are likened by the authors to which existing dangerousness criterion?
mcqs.e: They draw on the 'grave disability' criteria used in assessing dangerousness to self, paralleling hoarding deficits.

authors: Andrew E Hoet, S Swisher, S Tomasi, T Fentie, A Melaku, S Nigatu, A Mengistu, A Assefa, Jeanette O'Quin, Jason W Stull, Wondwossen Gebreyes, Christina T Hammons, Amanda Berrian

mcqs.q: How many WOAH Day One Competencies does the evaluation tool assess?
mcqs.e: The tool systematically measures proficiency across all 19 WOAH Day One Competencies.

mcqs.q: The evaluation tool is designed to be used alongside what to give a full picture of competency coverage?
mcqs.e: It is meant to be paired with curriculum mapping to show how effectively competencies are taught and to identify gaps.

mcqs.q: Where was the tool developed and tested?
mcqs.e: It was developed and tested at the University of Gondar College of Veterinary Medicine in Ethiopia.

authors: Kristin Jankowski, J Claire Schuch, Kaitlyn V Andres, Julie K Levy, Terry G Spencer

mcqs.q: In 2025, spectrum of care (SOC) subcompetencies were added to veterinary curricula by which body?
o: The AAVMC Spectrum of Care Initiative Task Force (into CBVE outcomes)
mcqs.e: The AAVMC SOC Task Force added SOC subcompetencies to the Competency-Based Veterinary Education learning outcomes.

mcqs.q: What was the main result of the online SOC coursework among the 121 students?
o: Statistically significant self-efficacy gains in 25 of 26 mapped questions
mcqs.e: Paired pre/post responses showed significant gains for 25 of the 26 questions mapped to SOC subcompetencies.

mcqs.q: What did the study conclude about distance education for this content?
o: It is ineffective for didactic material
It can consistently deliver didactic SOC content across multiple colleges, freeing clinical time
mcqs.e: Distance education delivered SOC content consistently across colleges while meeting AVMA COE accreditation standards.

authors: Marilize Van der Walt, Sarah E Jones, Julie K Levy, Emma Hart, Rosa Negash, Wendy M Novicoff, Nicole Jacque, Samantha J M Evans

mcqs.q: What was the 12-week survival rate for retrovirus-positive cats treated with GS-441524 for presumptive effusive FIP?
mcqs.e: Survival was 94% (16/17) at 12 weeks; 82% (14/17) survived to one year.

mcqs.q: Compared with FeLV-positive cats, FIV-positive cats developed FIP:
o: At a younger age and sooner after infection
At an older age and longer after retrovirus infection
Only in the presence of neoplasia
mcqs.e: FIV cats developed FIP at an older age and a longer interval after retrovirus infection than FeLV cats.

mcqs.q: What was the overall conclusion about treating retrovirus-positive cats for FIP?
o: Therapy is contraindicated in retrovirus-positive cats
Treatment success was similar to outcomes reported for FIP alone
mcqs.e: Outcomes resembled prior FIP-alone results; retrovirus status did not preclude remission, though many cats later died of neoplasia.

authors: Melissa J Beall, Dana Moore, Sean Turner, Julie K Levy
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery

mcqs.q: Which sample type was most sensitive for point-of-care SNAP FeLV antigen testing?
mcqs.e: Whole blood on SNAP detected more low-positive cats than plasma or serum and is the preferred sample.

mcqs.q: How did long-term survival compare between high-positive and low-positive FeLV cats?
o: High-positive cats had higher early mortality while most low-positive cats survived
Low-positive cats died early while high-positive cats survived
mcqs.e: 19/29 (66%) low-positive cats were still alive versus only 2.2% of high-positive cats, which carry high early-mortality risk.

mcqs.q: What is the clinical implication of combining whole-blood antigen, PetChek, and qPCR results?
o: Classifying cats as high/low/cryptic supports managing FeLV as a chronic condition
Adoption of FeLV-positive cats should stop
mcqs.e: Classification into high-, low-positive, or cryptic guides prognosis and supports managing FeLV as a chronic disease.

authors: Emma K LaVigne, Nicole E Levy, Alexis R Bardzinski, Federica Scaletti, Kevin Horecka, Mia K Cuccinello, Dana M Moore, Julie K Levy

mcqs.q: Was a spectrum-of-care diagnostic approach (exam, CBC, chemistry, FeLV antigen, without advanced imaging/PCR) adequate to treat shelter cats for FIP?
o: Yes, it was sufficient and preserved resources
mcqs.e: The spectrum-of-care approach was sufficient to treat shelter FIP with GS-441524 while conserving resources.

mcqs.q: How did FIP remission and treatment-period survival compare between FeLV-positive and FeLV-negative cats?
o: Equivalent FIP remission and treatment-period survival
mcqs.e: Remission rates and treatment-period survival (79% vs 76%) were equivalent between the groups.

mcqs.q: Despite equivalent FIP remission, FeLV-positive cats experienced:
o: Significantly shorter overall survival (median 524 days) from FeLV
mcqs.e: FeLV-positive cats had significantly shorter overall survival driven by underlying FeLV infection, despite equal FIP remission.

authors: Kim Valenta, Tsiky Rajaonarivelo, Angelique Ferreira, Ange Raharinirina, Radoniaina R Rafaliarison, Alisha Farris, Jonas M Watson, Susan deFrance, Dominic Mayo, Caitlynn Filla, Abigail Ross, Sally L Bornbusch, Siddharth Satishchandran, Thomas Kelly, Julie K Levy, Zoavina Randriana, Zach J Farris

mcqs.q: After habitat loss, what does the article cite as the second greatest threat to biodiversity?
mcqs.e: Invasive species such as free-roaming domestic dogs are described as the second greatest biodiversity threat after habitat loss.

mcqs.q: How did free-roaming dogs around Madagascar's protected areas affect wildlife?
o: Through predation, displacement, and vectoring pathogens and antimicrobial resistance
mcqs.e: Dogs predated and displaced wildlife and acted as vectors of pathogens and antimicrobial resistance.

mcqs.q: What intervention does the Mad Dog Initiative employ?
o: Humane reduction of free-roaming dog populations
mcqs.e: The Mad Dog Initiative humanely reduces free-roaming dog populations to lessen their impact on lemurs and wildlife.

authors: Simone D Guerios, Gina Clemmer, Julie K Levy

mcqs.q: Did HQHVSN spay/neuter capacity rebound after the COVID-19 lockdown?
o: No, it continued to decline and the deficit grew
mcqs.e: Clinics performed even fewer surgeries per quarter in follow-up than in 2021; capacity did not rebound.

mcqs.q: To approximately what figure did the estimated cumulative U.S. spay/neuter deficit rise?
mcqs.e: The cumulative deficit was estimated at 3.7 million surgeries, up from the prior 2.7 million projection.

mcqs.q: The authors warn that this sustained decline threatens:
o: Progress controlling pet overpopulation and access to preventive care
mcqs.e: Continued loss of low-cost spay/neuter undermines pet overpopulation control and access to basic preventive care.

authors: Champayne Danae Master, Marjorie Robin Vincent, Bridgid Ann Twomey, Claudia Vazquez, Jyothi Vinnakota Robertson

mcqs.q: Whom did community members identify as trusted connectors that the clinic then partnered with?
mcqs.e: Residents pointed to promotoras as trusted sources, so the clinic built relationships with them to link people to care.

mcqs.q: What clinic model resulted from the bilingual community needs assessments?
o: A Saturday-only clinic with bilingual services and off-site clinics in targeted zip codes
mcqs.e: The restructuring produced a Saturday-only model with bilingual services, outreach, and off-site clinics in targeted areas.

mcqs.q: What is the case study's key lesson for equitable veterinary access programs?
o: Use inclusive needs assessments, community partnerships, and culturally relevant delivery
mcqs.e: Inclusive assessments, partnerships, and culturally relevant service delivery underpin equitable, sustainable programs.

journal: Journal of Shelter Medicine and Community Animal Health (2025 ABVP Abstracts, Vol. 4 No. S1)

mcqs.q: Per this ABVP abstract, what was the key positive driver of shelter veterinarian job satisfaction?
mcqs.e: Among 94 California shelter veterinarians, the leading positive factor was making a meaningful impact.

mcqs.q: Which were identified as key negative factors for shelter veterinarian job satisfaction?
o: Lack of support staff, inability to meet animals' behavioral needs, and challenging leadership relationships
mcqs.e: Dissatisfaction was driven by inadequate support staff, inability to meet behavioral needs, and poor leadership relationships.

mcqs.q: How do the authors recommend improving veterinarian retention?
mcqs.e: They recommend operational efficiencies and crowding reduction rather than relying on compensation alone.
